summaries.example: Imagine two children disagree about whether sharing is good. A moral naturalist might say that the goodness of sharing is a real feature of the world, not just a feeling. The naturalist then asks whether this moral feature is connected to natural facts, such as how sharing helps people cooperate and flourish.
summaries.summary: Moral naturalism is a theory about what moral facts are. It says that facts about right and wrong, goodness, and reasons for acting are real facts that do not depend only on someone's opinion. It also says these facts belong to the natural world rather than to a supernatural world or a completely separate kind of reality. The difficult part is explaining exactly what “natural” means. Some philosophers connect moral properties with facts that science can investigate. Others connect them with human life, flourishing, reasons, or the causes and effects of actions. The entry also discusses descriptivism, which says that some ordinary descriptive words can refer to moral properties, and reductivism, which says that moral properties reduce to another kind of property. These ideas are closely related to naturalism, but the source emphasizes that philosophers use all three terms in different ways. Moral naturalism has supporters because it joins belief in real morality with confidence in natural explanations. Critics ask whether natural facts can truly explain the reason-giving or action-guiding side of morality.
key_ideas: Moral naturalism combines moral realism with a naturalistic view of the world.
Naturalists say moral facts are natural facts, but philosophers disagree about what makes a fact natural.
Some naturalists connect goodness with facts about people, actions, cooperation, or flourishing.
Descriptivism and reductivism are related views, but the source explains that neither gives a completely uncontroversial definition of naturalism.
Philosophers disagree about whether science, careful thinking, or some other method gives us moral knowledge.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate asks what kind of world we live in and how we can know what is right. If moral facts are natural, moral thinking might be connected to evidence about people and the world. If they are not natural, we may need a different account of moral truth and moral knowledge. Understanding the debate also helps us see why people can agree that morality matters while disagreeing about where moral truth comes from.

important_terms.definition: The view that some moral facts, such as facts about right and wrong, are real and do not depend only on what people believe.
The view that moral facts are part of the natural world and can be understood in connection with natural facts.
A fact that does not become true or false just because someone believes or feels something about it.
The idea that moral words, such as “good” or “wrong,” may describe features of things rather than merely showing feelings.

questions_to_think_about: Can something be really good even if everyone dislikes it?
If sharing helps a group work well, does that prove sharing is morally good?
Are moral facts more like facts about health, or more like personal choices?
How could we find out whether a moral fact is part of nature?

summaries.example: Suppose a community discovers that a policy reliably increases trust, cooperation, and the ability of people to meet their needs. A Cornell realist might treat these effects as evidence about the policy's moral value, while a neo-Aristotelian might ask whether the policy supports characteristically human flourishing. A non-naturalist could accept the same evidence yet deny that the moral property is identical with any natural property. The example shows that philosophers may agree about evidence while disagreeing about what moral properties are.
summaries.summary: Moral naturalism is usually presented as a form of moral realism: moral facts are stance-independent, but they are also natural facts. The entry separates several claims that are often grouped together. Fact naturalism concerns moral facts; property naturalism concerns moral properties; methodological naturalism concerns how moral knowledge is acquired; and analytic naturalism concerns whether moral claims are synonymous with suitable descriptive or scientific claims. The distinction matters because a philosopher can accept one of these theses while rejecting another. Descriptivism holds that some descriptive terms refer to moral properties. Reductivism holds, in a broad and contested sense, that moral properties reduce to other properties. The source argues that neither view provides an easy definition of naturalism, partly because “reduction” has linguistic and metaphysical uses and because “natural” itself is difficult to characterize. Support for naturalism includes the thought that naturalism and moral realism are both attractive, arguments from moral supervenience, and the hope that naturalism can answer skeptical challenges about moral knowledge. Major objections include Moore's Open Question Argument, the Normativity Objection, and the Triviality Objection. The entry explains that the Open Question Argument most directly targets analytic descriptivism. It then surveys three influential naturalist programs: neo-Aristotelian naturalism, Cornell realism, and Jackson's analytic functionalism. Each attempts to explain moral properties while facing problems about normativity, language, evidence, or disagreement.
key_ideas: The entry distinguishes moral realism, fact naturalism, property naturalism, methodological naturalism, and analytic naturalism; these claims need not stand or fall together.
Analytic naturalists treat some moral-natural identities as discoverable through conceptual analysis, whereas synthetic naturalists treat them as substantive, empirically informed identities.
Supervenience motivates naturalism in two ways: naturalism appears to explain it directly, and some arguments try to infer natural identity from it.
The Open Question Argument is widely taken to challenge analytic descriptivism, but the entry explains why it does not straightforwardly refute synthetic naturalism or one-term naturalism.
Neo-Aristotelian naturalism explains goodness through kinds, characteristic forms of life, and human flourishing; Cornell realism explains moral properties through complex causal profiles.
Jackson's analytic functionalism identifies moral properties through a network of moral platitudes and asks what natural properties fulfill the resulting functional roles.
summaries.why_it_matters: Metaethics is not simply a debate about which actions are right. It asks what moral truth is, whether moral properties belong in a scientific picture of reality, and how moral knowledge is possible. These questions affect how we interpret moral disagreement, empirical evidence, moral reasoning, and skepticism. The entry also illustrates a broader philosophical lesson: a familiar label may cover several distinct theses, and clarifying those theses can be as important as defending or criticizing them.

important_terms.definition: The metaethical view that stance-independent moral facts or properties exist.
A form of moral realism holding that moral facts or properties are natural facts or properties.
The thesis that moral facts do not vary merely because an agent's beliefs, attitudes, or responses vary.
The view that some descriptive terms refer to moral properties, whether through conceptual analysis or through synthetic identity claims.
A contested thesis that moral properties reduce to, or are less fundamental than, other properties; philosophers disagree about the reduction relation.
The claim that there cannot be two possible worlds with the same natural facts but different moral facts.
The argument that a natural property cannot be identical with goodness because one can understand the proposed identity and still coherently ask whether it is true.
The view that moral terms refer to complex natural properties identified by their causal roles rather than by simple definitions.

questions_to_think_about: Does supervenience require moral properties to be identical with natural properties, or could another relation explain it?
Why might the Open Question Argument challenge analytic descriptivism without challenging every form of naturalism?
Can a property be natural and normative at the same time?
Would a moral disagreement between two communities show that their words have different meanings or that they disagree about the same moral facts?
What would count as good evidence for identifying a moral property?

summaries.example: Think about a school rule requiring students to return shared equipment. One student says the rule is good because returning equipment builds trust and helps everyone use the equipment later. A moral naturalist might say that these facts are part of what makes the rule morally good. Another philosopher might agree that the rule helps cooperation but deny that its usefulness is identical to its moral goodness. They agree about some effects but disagree about what goodness is.
summaries.summary: Moral naturalism is a position in metaethics, the part of philosophy that studies what moral claims mean, whether they are true, and how we know them. It combines moral realism—the view that there are real, stance-independent moral facts—with naturalism, the view that those facts are natural rather than supernatural or belonging to a separate non-natural realm. The entry shows that this simple description hides several questions. Are moral facts the same as natural facts? Are moral properties natural properties? Do we learn moral truths through methods similar to science? Are moral words secretly equivalent to descriptive words? Philosophers answer these questions differently. Descriptivism says some descriptive terms refer to moral properties. Reductivism says moral properties reduce to other properties, but “reduction” can mean different things. Supporters of naturalism point to the success of natural inquiry, the apparent objectivity of ordinary moral judgments, and the fact that moral facts seem to depend on natural facts. This last idea is called supervenience. Critics argue that natural facts describe how the world is, while moral facts also tell us what matters or what we have reason to do. Moore's Open Question Argument suggests that no natural property can simply be defined as goodness, although the entry explains why this argument may target only some forms of naturalism. Overall, the source presents moral naturalism as influential but conceptually difficult.
key_ideas: Naturalism says morality is part of the natural world, while non-naturalism says moral facts are a different kind of fact.
The word “natural” may refer to what science studies, to what fits a naturalistic worldview, or to how moral facts are known.
Analytic naturalism connects moral meanings to descriptive meanings; synthetic naturalism treats moral-natural identities as discoveries rather than definitions.
The Open Question Argument challenges the idea that goodness can simply be defined as pleasure or as some other natural property.
Naturalists answer that moral identities might be informative discoveries, or that moral properties may be complex and not captured by one simple definition.
The source presents support and objections rather than declaring one side settled.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate connects everyday moral judgment with deeper questions about science, objectivity, language, and human knowledge. It helps explain why someone might believe that morality is more than personal preference while still asking whether moral truth can be part of the natural world. It also teaches an important skill in philosophy: before arguing about a theory, clarify what its key terms mean.

important_terms.definition: The belief that moral truths are real and are not made true only by people's opinions or attitudes.
The view that real moral facts are also facts belonging to the natural world.
Not depending on what a person or group happens to believe, want, or approve of.
The view that some non-moral, descriptive words can refer to moral properties.
The view that moral properties can be understood as another kind of property, though philosophers disagree about what “reduce” means.
The idea that two possible worlds cannot match in all natural facts while differing in their moral facts.

questions_to_think_about: If two actions have exactly the same natural features, must they have the same moral value?
Is “good” more like “unmarried,” which is built into a definition, or more like “water,” which required investigation?
Can facts about cooperation or human flourishing explain why something gives us a reason to act?
Does disagreement about morality show that there are no objective moral facts?
